4.2.1. The non-competition clause agreed upon in the purchase agreement of December 18, 2020, 
reads as follows with respect to the defendants:  
"5.1 A.________ and Sevenedge AG are prohibited from using the name components ‘Prime,’ 
'GetTemp,‘ 'Construction,’ 
‘Care,’ and ‘21’ to compete with B.________ AG.  
5.2 Likewise, A.________, his new employer, and all companies affiliated with him are 
prohibited from presenting themselves on the market in the name of B.________ AG or its 
trademarks and subsidiaries, and from using the aforementioned name components ‘Prime,’ 
'GetTemp,‘ 'Construction,’  
‘Care’—either alone or in combination with any number—as well as ‘21’ to compete with 
B.________ AG or to imply any connection to his former affiliation with B.________ AG.  
Exceptions to this include (a) references to the past in the personal résumés of A.________ and 
all employees of his affiliated companies, particularly on social media, as well as (b) situations in 
which such information is unavoidable in order to fulfill legal and contractual obligations toward 
third parties, as is particularly required for data protection-related information regarding the 
origin of personal data or for contract amendments with customers, landlords, and other third 
parties necessary for the execution of this agreement. 
5.3 For each individual instance of a breach of Sections 5.1 and 5.2, A.________ and/or 
Sevenedge AG shall owe a contractual penalty of CHF 100,000. Payment of the contractual 
penalty does not release the party from compliance with the non-competition clause or from 
liability for consequential damages.” 
4.2.2. The lower court held that it was undisputed and in accordance with the parties’ mutual 
intent that a letter to the experts at Construction21 AG—both in general and with regard to its 
specific content—was permissible only to the extent that it was indispensable for informing third 
parties.
